sections.title: 1. Types of adverse reactions

blocks.title: Types of adverse reaction (A-E)
rows: e.g. **lithium** toxicity - ataxia, coarse tremors, vomiting
Idiosyncratic, e.g. malignant hyperthermia, or **lamotrigine**-induced Steven Johnson syndrome
Related to cumulative drug use, e.g. long term **lithium** use and renal damage
Not due to dose per se but due to the length of use of a medication, e.g. tardive dyskinesia in some cases
Related to abrupt discontinuation, e.g. **SSRI** discontinuation reaction, opioid withdrawal effects

blocks.mnemonic: Augmented, Bizarre, Continuous use, Delayed, End of use
expansion: C: Continuous use (dose and time related)

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Tolerance is the need to use increased doses of a drug to maintain a clinical effect; it is seen for both therapeutic effects and side effects.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Tolerance may be due to decreased sensitivity of the target receptors through down-regulation (fewer receptors, in the case of agonists), up-regulation (more receptors, in the case of antagonists), or reduced responsivity without any change in receptor numbers.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Drugs with similar pharmacological actions can show cross-tolerance, e.g. benzodiazepines and barbiturates.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Sensitization (reverse tolerance) is when sensitivity to a drug effect increases over time, so the same dose produces more pronounced effects as treatment progresses; it is reported with street use of cocaine.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Up- or down-regulation can also be a mechanism of therapeutic effect: with SSRIs, the 5HT1A autoreceptors in somatodendritic zones downregulate secondary to the increased serotonin availability when reuptake is blocked, which increases the serotonergic tone of the neurons.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Type A = Augmented (dose-related), e.g. lithium toxicity; Type B = Bizarre (non-dose related, idiosyncratic), e.g. malignant hyperthermia, lamotrigine SJS.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Type C = Continuous use (dose and time related), e.g. long-term lithium and renal damage; Type D = Delayed, e.g. tardive dyskinesia; Type E = End of use (withdrawal).

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Tolerance = need for higher doses to keep an effect (seen for therapeutic and side effects); via down-regulation, up-regulation or reduced responsivity.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Cross-tolerance between similar drugs, e.g. benzodiazepines and barbiturates; sensitization (reverse tolerance) is seen with street cocaine.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: SSRIs: 5HT1A somatodendritic autoreceptor downregulation raises serotonergic tone - a therapeutic use of receptor regulation.

sections.title: 1b. Withdrawal and discontinuation reactions

blocks.text: When drugs are given for a reasonable period a physiological adaptation develops, which can be disturbed on withdrawal and lead to withdrawal symptoms. Abrupt withdrawal, especially of an agent with a shorter elimination half-life, leads to clinically significant withdrawal symptoms.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Hypnotics, opiates, barbiturates, SSRIs and **venlafaxine** are some of the drugs associated with discontinuation reaction or withdrawal symptoms.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.title: Variables influencing withdrawal symptoms
rows: **Methadone** has less withdrawal than heroin as **methadone** has a longer t1/2
**Paroxetine** has anticholinergic properties; withdrawal causes cholinergic rebound symptoms
**Paroxetine** inhibits its own metabolism via **CYP2D6**, so withdrawal leads to loss of inhibition, excessive **paroxetine** breakdown, a sudden steep drop in levels and withdrawal symptoms
**Fluoxetine** has an active metabolite, norfluoxetine, with a long half-life, so it produces fewer withdrawal symptoms
Slow, gradual tapering is best; ==10%== dose reduction every 2 weeks is advocated for benzodiazepines

An enzyme inducer can reduce a drug's effects acutely if its metabolism depends on the induced enzyme; an antagonist can precipitate withdrawal - the rationale for leaving at least 72 hours before prescribing **naltrexone** for an opioid detoxified patient
Full agonists produce more discontinuation reactions than partial agonists, e.g. **clonazepam** produces lesser benzodiazepine withdrawal symptoms

sources.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Sustained-release preparations change absorption kinetics, not elimination kinetics, so on withdrawal plasma levels fall at the same rate with XL and plain preparations; e.g. **venlafaxine** XL has a similar discontinuation reaction to normal-release **venlafaxine**. Depot preparations have less withdrawal propensity than the corresponding oral drugs.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Abrupt withdrawal after a reasonable period of use, especially of a short half-life drug, causes withdrawal symptoms.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Drugs associated: hypnotics, opiates, barbiturates, SSRIs, venlafaxine.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Longer t1/2 (methadone vs heroin) or long-half-life active metabolite (fluoxetine/norfluoxetine) = less withdrawal.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Paroxetine: anticholinergic (cholinergic rebound) and inhibits its own CYP2D6 metabolism, so levels drop steeply on withdrawal.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Taper slowly: 10% dose reduction every 2 weeks for benzodiazepines; leave at least 72 hours before naltrexone after opioid detoxification.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Full agonists cause more withdrawal than partial agonists; XL venlafaxine withdraws like normal-release; depots have less withdrawal than oral drugs.

sections.title: 2. Mechanism of adverse effects

blocks.title: Side effect and the receptor mechanism given
rows: **D2** blockade, 5HT2A stimulation (hence some data on **mirtazapine**, a 5HT2A antagonist, reducing akathisia)
Antimuscarinic action; in serotonin syndrome, may be mediated via 5HT2A/2C
alpha1 stimulation, 5HT2A stimulation (hence SSRIs cause insomnia)
**SWS** is maintained by 5HT2A inhibition; 5HT2A stimulation disrupts sleep architecture
Cholinergic effect and increases with noradrenaline reuptake inhibition
Blurred vision, exacerbation of narrow-angle glaucoma, delirium, and photophobia due to mydriasis, dry secretions, constipation, tachycardia, decreased sweating, urinary retention and hyperthermia
alpha1 antagonism, 5HT2A/2C stimulation (delayed ejaculation in SSRIs); retrograde ejaculation due to alpha1 block, anticholinergic and antihistaminic effects
Supersensitivity of dopamine receptors, which develops because of prolonged therapy with dopamine-blocking drugs
alpha2 blockade, 5HT2A/2C stimulation; 5HT2A/2C stimulation can also reduce libido
5HT1D stimulation can induce obsessions; 5HT1A and 2A stimulation reduce **OCD**
Habituation of dopamine receptors on repeated use of dopamine agonists (e.g. **levodopa**) leading to dopamine dysregulation syndrome (**DDS**)

sources.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Weight gain: no single mechanism explains this complex metabolic phenomenon. Antihistaminic effects, 5HT2A/2C antagonism and insulin resistance (**valproate** and **olanzapine**) are noted.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Genetic factors seem to involve the 5-**HT2C** receptor: drugs with a strong 5-**HT2C** affinity will have a greater impact on body weight in patients with a specific variant of polymorphism of the 5-**HT2C** receptor promoter regions.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Low-potency antipsychotics (**chlorpromazine** and thioridazine) produce more weight gain and sedation than high-potency agents (**haloperidol** and **fluphenazine**).

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Notes and bank differ on the 5HT2C wording. The notes give weight gain as 5HT2C antagonism (and antihistaminic effects). **Q26** (patient who does not want to be obese) has the keyed answer '5HT-2C agonism' as the profile to avoid, while **Q23** lists 5HT2-C antagonism among the mechanisms of antipsychotic weight gain and 5HT2-A antagonism as the one that is **NOT**. Learn the notes' direction (antagonism) and treat **Q26**'s wording with caution.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Q23**: of the proposed mechanisms of antipsychotic weight gain - 5HT2-C antagonism, H-1 antagonism, hyperprolactinaemia and increased serum leptin (secondary leptin desensitisation) - 5HT2-A antagonism is the one that is **NOT** a mechanism.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Q22**: sedation (and weight gain) from tricyclics is antihistaminic; dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision and glaucoma are the anticholinergic effects - so sedation is the one not due to anticholinergic blockade.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Q47**: postural hypotension with tricyclics is due to alpha-adrenergic (alpha-1) blockade.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Q8**: **SSRI** sexual side effects relate to 5HT2 (5HT2A) stimulation; agents with 5HT2A antagonist activity (e.g. **mirtazapine**) have a relatively low likelihood of sexual side effects.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Q2**: initial anxiety/agitation on SSRIs is proposed to be over-stimulation of 5HT2 receptors in the limbic system (far from conclusive); **fluoxetine** has high anxiogenic effect, **citalopram** the least.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Q70**: the toxic confusional state caused by antipsychotics is due to muscarinic receptor blockade.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

bullets.text: Agitation: alpha2 blockade, 5HT2A/2C stimulation; akathisia: D2 blockade plus 5HT2A stimulation (mirtazapine may reduce it).

sections.title: 3a. Antipsychotics - extrapyramidal effects and tardive dyskinesia

blocks.text: Acute extrapyramidal syndromes (acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism) are noted with high-potency drugs more than low-potency drugs. Tardive dyskinesia and dystonia and perioral tremor (rabbit syndrome) are chronic late side effects.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **PET** studies indicate that ==60%==-==80%== occupation of **D2** receptors is associated with antipsychotic efficacy. Higher occupancy is associated with increased risk of acute extrapyramidal symptoms and of hyperprolactinaemia (**D2** blockade on anterior pituitary mammotrophic cells, which are normally tonically inhibited by dopamine from the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus).

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Drugs prone to induce parkinsonism (**trifluoperazine**, **chlorpromazine**, raclopride, **haloperidol**, **fluphenazine**, **risperidone**) bind **D2** more tightly than dopamine; drugs with low parkinsonism-inducing propensity (**quetiapine**, **clozapine** etc.) bind more loosely than dopamine.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Loosely bound drugs are weaker in potency and need higher doses but can be titrated faster; they may dissociate from **D2** more rapidly and could lead to clinical relapse somewhat earlier than tightly bound drugs (though this does not seem to be the case for **clozapine**).

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.title: Acute and late movement syndromes with antipsychotics
rows: 15-==20%== of patients; within 90 days of treatment (5 to 90); elderly and female at higher risk
Muscle stiffness, cogwheel rigidity, shuffling gait, stooped posture, drooling; no pill-rolling tremor but a regular coarse tremor
Anticholinergics for a short period (up to 6 weeks); withdraw after 4 to 6 weeks as tolerance develops
Early in the treatment course; often younger men on a high dose of high-potency drugs; more common with **IM** administration

Brief or prolonged contractions of specific muscle groups: oculogyric crises, tongue protrusion, trismus, torticollis, blepharospasm; rarely pharyngeal dystonia (dysarthria, dysphagia, respiratory choking)
Spontaneous fluctuations; responds to reassurance and to anticholinergic drugs
Subjective and objective restlessness: inability to relax, jitteriness, pacing, rocking, alternating sitting and standing
Dose reduction, changing the drug, or adding a beta blocker, anticholinergic, benzodiazepine or cyproheptadine
Nearly ==25%== of patients; usually after at least 6 months, 1-2 years of treatment
Abnormal involuntary irregular choreoathetotic movements of head, limbs and trunk; perioral movements most common
Most cases remit spontaneously; **clozapine** can reduce the risk and treat it; dose reduction, withdrawal, switch to newer atypicals or add **clonazepam**
Late in the course of treatment
Tremor affecting the lips and perioral muscles

blocks.text: Drug-induced parkinsonism: low-potency drugs and those with higher anticholinergic effects cause less **EPSE**; more than ==80%== brain **D2** occupancy is thought to cause EPSEs. Atypicals cause low **EPSE** probably through anticholinergic effects, 5HT2A antagonism or less avidity of binding ('hit and run' profile especially for **clozapine** and **quetiapine**).

blocks.text: Longer chronic anticholinergic prescription increases the risk of **TD**.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Dystonia mechanism: dopaminergic hyperactivity in the basal ganglia when plasma levels fluctuate may be responsible. Dystonias can reduce compliance.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Akathisia (possibly due to higher **D2** occupancy in striatum) can be caused by neuroleptics, antidepressants and sympathomimetics, and may be associated with increased absconsion, suicides and violence if left undiagnosed and untreated.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: In serious cases of **TD** the breathing and swallowing muscles are involved, leading to aerophagia and grunting. **TD** is exacerbated by stress but absent during sleep; the lack of insight into the movement disorder is striking.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

rows: Affective illness rather than pure psychotic disorder
Frequent drug holidays - will lead to high dose prescription with each relapse

sources.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Elderly have a poor spontaneous resolution of **TD**; it is less likely to remit in elderly than in young patients.

sections.title: 3b. Antipsychotics - neuroleptic malignant syndrome

blocks.text: **NMS** can occur at any time during treatment with neuroleptics.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: It consists of the tetrad of extreme hyperthermia, severe muscular rigidity and confusion, and autonomic fluctuations (**BP** and pulse rate); patients may be akinetic and mute.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Increased **WBC** count, creatinine phosphokinase, liver enzymes, plasma myoglobin and myoglobinuria are noted.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.title: Course, risk factors and treatment of NMS (notes)
rows: Subacute onset in 24 to 72 hours; if untreated lasts 10 to 14 days
More common in young men, after agitation and when using high-potency drugs especially in rapid tranquillisation; dopaminergic drugs on withdrawal can produce **NMS**
May be related to dopamine blockade or hypothalamic sympathetic dysregulation
Around 20-==30%== if untreated, and higher if depot is used

Immediately stop the offending psychotropic; symptomatic management of vital sign instability, fluid replacement, prevention of renal failure secondary to myoglobinuria and of aspiration pneumonia; dantrolene, bromocriptine or amantadine can be used
A low-potency or atypical drug must be used following recovery for an antipsychotic prescription

sections.title: 3d. Antipsychotics - sexual dysfunction, hyperprolactinaemia and priapism

blocks.text: Increased dopaminergic transmission can enhance sexual arousal and penile erection. Antipsychotics reduce sexual performance both directly (reduced dopaminergic transmission) and indirectly through hyperprolactinaemia; ==43%== of those taking antipsychotics report sexual dysfunction at some point, not all attributable to the drug.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Hyperprolactinaemia can result in loss of sexual arousal and erectile dysfunction in men, and amenorrhoea, reduced sexual desire and hirsutism in women.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Neuroleptics commonly cause ejaculatory problems: total inhibition of ejaculation (dry ejaculation), reduced ejaculatory volume and retrograde ejaculation, with conventional neuroleptics and also **clozapine**, **risperidone** and **olanzapine**.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Nearly ==50%== of men taking antipsychotics report ejaculatory and erectile disturbances; thioridazine is particularly associated with decreased libido and retrograde ejaculation in men.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: The dopaminergic agonist bromocriptine is used to treat sexual dysfunction in men associated with hyperprolactinaemia.

rows: Simultaneous alpha1-adrenergic blockade and anticholinergic activity
Antipsychotic drugs (==20%== of all reported priapisms), followed by **trazodone**
Risk is dose-independent and can occur at any time during the course of treatment (duration-independent)
A urological emergency; can lead to permanent impotence if untreated

sections.title: 3e. Antipsychotics - other side effects (seizures, cardiac, QT, skin, eye, liver, depot injection)

blocks.text: Seizure threshold is lowered especially by low-potency antipsychotics; molindone may be the least epileptogenic. This is a dose-dependent effect.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **Chlorpromazine** is the most sedating typical antipsychotic (**H1** antihistaminic action); tolerance usually develops. Low-potency agents can also cause anticholinergic syndrome (see TCAs).

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Neuroleptics can decrease cardiac contractility, raise circulating catecholamines and prolong atrial and ventricular conduction time. Low-potency drugs are more cardiotoxic than high-potency drugs. **ECG** shows **QT** and **PR** prolongation, blunting of T waves and **ST** depression. Thioridazine and droperidol in particular can cause torsade de pointes.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Antipsychotic-related sudden death may be due to cardiac arrhythmias, or even seizures, asphyxiation or malignant hyperthermia; **QT**-prolonging drugs (e.g. thioridazine) are associated with more sudden deaths.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Postural hypotension is most common with low-potency drugs and tolerance develops soon; patients should avoid all caffeine and alcohol, drink plenty of fluid and take liberal salt in food. Low-potency drugs can cause weight gain, but not as much as atypical drugs.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **QT** prolongation is mediated by blockade of the rapid component of the delayed rectifier potassium current (IKr) responsible for repolarisation of cardiac Purkinje and myocardial cells. Droperidol, pimozide, sertindole and thioridazine have a greater capacity than other antipsychotics to cause IKr blockade.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

rows: Long-term use can cause blue-gray discoloration of sun-exposed skin; reversible
Pigmentation of anterior lens and posterior cornea: whitish brown stellate granular deposits on slit lamp; benign, not vision impairing; can resolve gradually
Irreversible retinal pigmentation with high dose (above 1000 mg a day); early symptom can be nocturnal confusion with difficulty with night vision; can progress even after stopping

sources.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Allergic dermatitis and photosensitivity can occur with low-potency agents.

blocks.text: **Chlorpromazine** is associated with obstructive or cholestatic jaundice, especially in the first month of treatment, with rash and eosinophilia; immediate discontinuation and avoidance of rechallenge are advised.

blocks.text: **Haloperidol** is one of the safest typical antipsychotics in overdose; after overdose the **EEG** shows diffuse slowing and low voltage.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Inadvertent intravascular injection (**IAIV**) / post-injection delirium sedation syndrome (**PDSS**) has been described after **olanzapine** pamoate depot injections: within 20 minutes to 3 hours, sedation, confusion, dizziness, altered speech/dysarthria and somnolence (as in oral **olanzapine** overdose); rarely deep coma. Supportive care usually gives full recovery within 3-72 hours.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: It is linked to accidental puncture of a vessel or injection into a rich capillary bed, causing quick dissolution and release of free **olanzapine**. Eli Lilly recommended a post-injection observation period of at least 1-3 hours in a healthcare facility and no driving or operating heavy machinery for 24 hours after injection.

blocks.text: Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of disorders comprising central/abdominal obesity, dyslipidaemias, glucose intolerance, insulin resistance (or hyperinsulinaemia) and hypertension. It is highly predictive of type 2 diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease.

blocks.text: Phase 2 (efficacy pathway): those who discontinued for ineffectiveness (re-randomised, n=99) compared **clozapine** with other atypicals. **Clozapine** had the lowest discontinuation rate - median 10 months, nearly 3 times longer than other SGAs. **Quetiapine** had comparatively less EPSEs.

blocks.text: Phase 2 (tolerance pathway): 444 volunteers who stopped phase 1 for intolerable side effects were tested with **olanzapine**, **risperidone**, **quetiapine** or **ziprasidone**; **olanzapine** and **risperidone** had equivalent effectiveness, both better than **quetiapine** or **ziprasidone** by significant but modest margins.

blocks.text: **TCA** side effects are related to anticholinergic, antihistaminic and antiadrenergic properties.

The most noradrenergic selective of the TCAs
**Amitriptyline** is associated with weight gain (antihistaminic effect; weight gain can also occur secondary to 5HT2C antagonism in other antidepressants)
TCAs are less likely to cause them than SSRIs

blocks.text: TCAs may cause **QT** prolongation; even at therapeutic doses they cause tachycardia, flattened T waves, prolonged **QT** intervals and depressed **ST** segment.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: TCAs are lethal in overdose, causing cardiac arrhythmias and anticholinergic delirium, which may occur 3-4 days after overdose due to the long half-life. There is no specific antidote; management needs lavage and **QRS** monitoring.

blocks.text: Amoxapine can cause hyperprolactinaemia as it has dopamine antagonistic effects. **SIADH** and hyponatraemia can occur with TCAs. Fine rapid tremor and dysarthria are sometimes reported.

blocks.text: **Amitriptyline**, **imipramine** and the non-tricyclic **mianserin** have been documented to precipitate an attack of angle-closure glaucoma.

sections.title: 4b. Serotonin syndrome (and NMS vs serotonin syndrome)

blocks.text: Serotonin syndrome results from excessive serotonergic transmission in the brain. No single mechanism explains all effects, but most **CNS** symptoms are possibly mediated via 5HT2A receptor stimulation.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Features: diarrhoea, myoclonus, diaphoresis, hyperactive reflexes, ataxia, hypomanic or labile mood, tremors and disorientation. It may mimic **NMS** or anticholinergic syndrome in those receiving psychotropics.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.title: Drugs with a high risk of serotonin syndrome (notes)
rows: **SSRI** and **TCA** antidepressants, fenfluramine, **LSD**, ecstasy, anti-migraine drugs (e.g. sumatriptan)
**SSRI** + **MAOI** or **RIMA** or another **SSRI**; serotonergic TCAs; SNRIs; **lithium**; l-tryptophan; **TCA** + **MAOI**
Tramadol, pethidine, meperidine on combination with the above agents
Linezolid (oxazolidinone antibacterial; reversible non-selective **MAOI**), tetrabenazine (dopamine and serotonin depletion), entacapone (**COMT** inhibitor), selegiline

sources.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Treatment of serotonin syndrome: withdraw the offending agent; supportive care (correct vital signs); benzodiazepines; 5HT2A antagonists - cyproheptadine, atypical antipsychotics, **chlorpromazine** (**mirtazapine** controversial); in severe cases neuromuscular paralysis and intubation.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.title: NMS vs serotonin syndrome
rows: Dopamine antagonism and suspected hypothalamic-mediated sympathetic overdrive
Resolves in 2 weeks, depending on t1/2 of offending drug
Resolves as soon as excess serotonin is reduced - generally in 24 hours
These laboratory abnormalities are less frequent

sections.title: 4c. Antidepressants - SSRIs

blocks.text: Nausea, vomiting, anorexia and diarrhoea are common **SSRI** side effects; somewhat dose-dependent and lessened by dose reduction or slower titration.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: SSRIs (like TCAs, but less often) cause weight gain in up to ==30%== of patients, especially in long-term maintenance. Insomnia and anorexia are often present initially; desensitisation and down-regulation of receptors may explain the reversal of the initial appetite-suppressing effect, leading to late weight gain.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Sexual difficulties - reduced libido, impotence, ejaculatory dysfunction and anorgasmia - are reported with SSRIs; incidence is nearly ==1 in 3== treated patients.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Akathisia-like effects, EPSEs and galactorrhoea are rarely reported; **fluoxetine** is associated with a change in duration of the menstrual period (significance unknown).

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: SSRIs can cause functional impairment of platelet aggregation (thrombasthenia) but not a reduction in platelet number, causing easy bruising or prolonged bleeding in those with gastric ulcers or bleeding diathesis.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **SIADH** is also reported - often troublesome in alcoholics and the elderly - causing hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, serum hypo-osmolality and increased urine osmolality. Stopping the offending drug, demeclocycline and fluid restriction can help.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Severe sweating, especially nocturnal, is seen in some patients; terazosin is effective in counteracting sweating.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Nocturnal myoclonus (repetitive leg movements every 20 to 60 seconds, with extension of the large toe and flexion of ankle, knee and hips) is reported; benzodiazepines and **levodopa** may be tried. Restless leg syndrome (creeping deep sensations with irresistible urge to move the legs) is associated with SSRIs; **ropinirole** or benzodiazepines and **levodopa** can treat it.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **Duloxetine**, **venlafaxine**, **citalopram**, **fluoxetine** and **paroxetine** can induce acute angle-closure glaucoma; the mechanism is unclear (anticholinergic effects or increased serotonin causing partial pupillary dilation have been implicated).

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **SSRI** discontinuation syndrome: abrupt withdrawal, especially of **paroxetine** (additional cholinergic rebound) or **fluvoxamine** (shorter half-life). It usually requires at least 4-6 weeks of treatment before discontinuation and resolves spontaneously in 3 weeks; those with significant **SSRI** intolerance at onset have more discontinuation reactions.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **Fluoxetine** is the **SSRI** least likely to cause withdrawal because its metabolite has a half-life of more than 1 week, giving slow self-tapering; it can even be used to treat or prevent discontinuation syndrome when stopping another **SSRI**, though a delayed withdrawal syndrome has been reported with **fluoxetine**.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.title: SSRI discontinuation syndrome - criteria (as in the notes)
rows: Discontinuation or reduction of dose of **SSRI** after at least 1 month of use

Two or more of the following within 1-7 days of criterion A, causing significant functional impairment and not due to a general medical condition: dizziness, lightheadedness, shock-like sensations (paraesthesias), diarrhoea, fatigue, gait instability, headache, insomnia, nausea, tremors, visual disturbances

blocks.text: Suicide risk and SSRIs: in short-term (4 to 16 weeks) placebo-controlled trials of nine antidepressants in those up to age 24, the average risk of suicidal thinking or behaviour in the first few months was ==4%== on antidepressants versus ==2%== on placebo.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Ecological studies: for every ==10%== rise in **SSRI** prescription, a ==3%== decline in suicide rates in certain countries; patients were significantly more likely to attempt/commit suicide in the month before starting drug therapy than in the 6 months after. The issue remains controversial, and **MHRA** has advised against certain **SSRI** prescriptions in children and adolescents.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: SSRIs increase the risk of upper **GI** bleeding, especially in the elderly and **NSAID** users: they inhibit serotonin uptake into platelets (serotonin is crucial for platelet aggregation) and increase gastric acid secretion, raising risk of erosion, ulcer and bleeding. Alcohol intake and H. pylori positivity increase the risk further.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Antidepressants with low inhibition of serotonin reuptake (**nortriptyline**, **doxepin**, **trazodone**) are safer for **GI** bleeding than those with high inhibition (**clomipramine**, **paroxetine**, **sertraline**, **fluoxetine**).

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Sexual dysfunction follows increased serotonergic neurotransmission. **Bupropion**, **mirtazapine**, **moclobemide**, **nefazodone** and **reboxetine** may have a relatively lower incidence; 5-**HT2** antagonists (cyproheptadine, **mirtazapine**), 5-HT1a agonists (**buspirone**) and **bupropion** (a dopamine reuptake inhibitor) can reverse **SSRI**-related sexual dysfunction.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **Sildenafil** (phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor; cGMP mediates penile vasodilatation) has been tried successfully for **SSRI**-induced erectile dysfunction. Side effects: headache (most common), dizziness, blurred vision, blue tinge to vision; very rarely priapism. Avoid in arrhythmias, unstable angina or uncontrolled hypertension.

blocks.title: Other antidepressants - side-effect profile (notes)
rows: Sweating more common than with SSRIs (treated by terazosin); above 300 mg/day significant numbers have a rise in diastolic **BP** (not restricted to those with pre-existing hypertension); mydriasis and angle-closure glaucoma; significant discontinuation reactions because of short half-life - taper gradually over 2-4 weeks
Side effects similar to **venlafaxine** but fewer propensities to affect blood pressure
Priapism, serious if unattended; emergency step is intracavernosal injection of an alpha1 agonist such as metaraminol or epinephrine; risk greatest in the early phase of treatment

Inhibits **CYP3A4** and can cause serious hepatic damage (so less used now); alpha1 antiadrenergic effects can produce pseudo-anticholinergic symptoms; afterimage formation (**LSD**-like tracking phenomenon) in up to ==12%==
Both have a favourable profile for the elderly and those with cardiac illness

No anticholinergic effects, no sedation or weight gain, almost negligible sexual side effects, no orthostatic hypotension or cardiac effects; can exacerbate **ADHD**, eating disorders and tics; can enhance sexual activity; seizure risk dose-dependent; commonest: headache, insomnia, dry mouth, tremor, nausea; can exacerbate severe anxiety or panic; can cause psychotic symptoms, delirium and word-finding difficulties

Agranulocytosis reported (signs of infection need prompt follow-up); with **mianserin**: drowsiness in first weeks, low propensity for orthostatic hypotension or cardiac effects, increased weight gain and appetite, minimal sexual effects; 5-**HT3** blockade reduces nausea and vomiting so it is preferred for depression with cancer chemotherapy

Can raise **haloperidol** concentrations; with **MAOI** can cause serotonin syndrome (2-week washout recommended); **CYP3A4** inhibitors (erythromycin, itraconazole, **nefazodone**, grapefruit juice) raise levels; no weight gain, sexual dysfunction, discontinuation symptoms, significant sleep disturbance or sedation

**NARI** with negligible serotonergic effects, safe cardiovascular profile, usable in the elderly; urinary hesitancy in around ==10%== of male trial patients, relieved by tamsulosin or doxazosin (**atomoxetine** is the same group but used in **ADHD**)

Weight gain and sexual dysfunction are also reported.

blocks.title: Cheese (tyramine) reaction
rows: MAOIs plus tyramine (and other monoamine) rich foods
Tyramine has direct and indirect (vesicular release) sympathomimetic actions, developing 20 min to 1 h after ingestion

Nausea, apprehension, occasional chills, sweating, restlessness and hypotension with occipital headache, palpitations and vomiting; sympathetic overdrive shows as piloerection, dilated pupils and fever; if severe, cerebral haemorrhage and death can occur
Safer in frequency and severity of hypertensive crisis
Mature cheese such as Stilton, blue cheese, old cheddar and mozzarella; fish, cured meats, sausage; mature poultry, wild game; liqueurs; concentrated yeast extract
Alpha-adrenergic antagonists such as phentolamine, or **chlorpromazine** (available on most wards); lowers **BP** in a few minutes

sections.title: 5a. Antimanic agents - lithium adverse effects

blocks.title: Lithium - renal effects
rows: Associated with peak **lithium** levels; once-daily rather than twice-daily dosing can reduce it; nearly 1/3rd of those treated have it, tolerance develops in due course; underlying mechanism is functional antagonism of **ADH** by **lithium** ion
K+-sparing diuretics such as amiloride or spironolactone

May occur in severe, prolonged toxicity, but cumulative **lithium** use rather than toxicity more commonly leads to renal failure; exposure longer than 10 years induces interstitial fibrosis and chronic renal damage

sources.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **Lithium** has a narrow therapeutic index. Toxicity occurs in overdose or dehydration; non-specific **GI** symptoms usually precede the more serious neurological symptoms and renal shutdown. Stop **lithium** immediately and seek urgent medical attention; haemodialysis may be required if levels exceed 4 mEq/L.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Cardiac: **ECG** effects of a therapeutic dose resemble hypokalaemia - flat or inverted T waves. **Lithium** can depress sinus node activity and is contraindicated in sick sinus syndrome.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.title: Lithium - thyroid effects
rows: A benign hypothyroid state; ==5%== may develop goitre; overt hyperthyroidism also reported in some
Common in those at risk through pre-existing antithyroid antibodies (especially middle-aged women); risk 3-4:1 in women; high in the first 2 years; rapid cycling patients at higher risk
High **TSH** in nearly 1/3rd of chronic **lithium**-treated patients even without clinical hypothyroidism
In resistant depression and non-responsive rapid cyclers, thyroxine for subclinical hypothyroidism may benefit mood

sources.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf
paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Haematological: **lithium** can cause leucocytosis, which is therapeutically utilised in some cases of benign neutropenia related to **clozapine** (not widely practised).

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Neurological: fine tremor is a common benign side effect; coarse tremor is a sign of toxicity. **Propranolol** can treat **lithium**-induced fine tremor at therapeutic levels.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Teratogenic: the most common effect involves the cardiac valves, especially Ebstein's anomaly of the tricuspid valve; risk in **lithium**-exposed fetuses is 1 of 1,000 (20 times the general population). **Lithium**'s teratogenic effects are somewhat lower than those of **valproate** or **carbamazepine**.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **Lithium** is excreted into breast milk; signs of **lithium** toxicity in infants include lethargy, cyanosis and sluggish neonatal reflexes.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Skin: exacerbation of acne and psoriasis. Alopecia/hair loss occurs in 5 to 10 percent; it is not clear whether zinc and selenium supplementation can reverse or prevent it.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.title: Lithium - where the bank differs from or adds to the notes

items.text: Polyuria: notes say nearly 1/3rd of patients; **Q67** says polyuria from impaired urinary concentrating ability occurs in up to ==20%== of chronically treated patients. Both agree amiloride (K+-sparing) is the diuretic to use - thiazides can dramatically raise plasma **lithium** levels.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

items.text: Hypothyroidism: notes say especially middle-aged women (3-4:1 in women, first 2 years). **Q75**: **lithium**-induced hypothyroidism is keyed as much more common in **YOUNG** **FEMALES** (explanation: especially younger women). Disagreement - know both.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

items.text: Ebstein anomaly: notes say ==1 in 1==,000 (20 times the general population). **Q56**: more recent data suggest the effect is much smaller - best estimate 2-3 times (not 20-400 times as first suggested); general population risk 7:100,000; keyed true statement is that maternal mental illness in general may increase the risk; cardiac malformations ==2.41%== vs ==1.15%== (**RR** 1.65), dose-dependent.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

items.text: **Q36**: common and early **lithium** side effect = fine tremor (early **GI** upset too); coarse tremor signals toxicity (with weakness/twitching, drowsiness, confusion, ataxia).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

items.text: **Q83**: long-term **lithium** is nephrotoxic ('creatinine creep'); ==95%== excreted unchanged in urine; also nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and permanent histological change.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

blocks.note: **Q41** states **ACE** inhibitors raise **lithium** levels (reduced thirst, increased renal sodium loss; from no increase to four-fold), with a seven-fold higher risk of hospitalisation for **lithium** toxicity in the elderly, so eGFR and **lithium** level need closer monitoring. The notes list **ACE** inhibitors only in the psychiatric-effects table.

bullets.text: Lithium polyuria: peak-level related, nearly 1/3rd, ADH antagonism; once-daily dosing and amiloride/spironolactone help.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Renal failure is more often cumulative use (over 10 years: interstitial fibrosis) than toxicity.

sections.title: 5b. Antimanic agents - valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine and other anticonvulsants

blocks.title: Carbamazepine vs valproate - dose-related and idiosyncratic effects
rows: Visual disturbances, **GI** disturbances, cognitive impairment, vertigo and dizziness
Haematological reactions including agranulocytosis or aplastic anaemia, idiosyncratic Stevens-Johnson syndrome, fulminant hepatic damage and pancreatitis; **SIADH** is more common in the elderly
Hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, rash and rarely acute dermatitis

sources.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **SIADH** may be seen with **valproate**, though more common with **carbamazepine**; it is dose-dependent. **Oxcarbazepine** (10-keto derivative of **CBZ**) has an identical profile with less enzyme induction and fewer drug-drug interactions; less rash and neurotoxicity but more hyponatraemia than **CBZ**.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **Topiramate** is a weak inhibitor of carbonic anhydrase and can promote renal stones.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.title: Haematological effects
rows: Around ==10%== have gradual-onset leucopenia in the first 3 months; reversible on continued treatment or dose reduction
Thrombocytopenia is dose-related; reduce the dose if bruising or bleeding gums

sources.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Neurological: **lamotrigine** is generally well tolerated but can cause dizziness, ataxia, headache, sedation, tremor and nausea. **Topiramate** can produce word-finding difficulties (anomia) and poor concentration. **Vigabatrin** (no significant antimanic efficacy) has the peculiar side effect of visual field defects.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **Valproate** and the liver: **valproate** inhibits hepatic enzymes; acute liver injury is rare in practice. 5 to 40 percent have a persistent but clinically insignificant elevation of transaminases up to 3 times the upper limit of normal ('transaminitis'), usually asymptomatic and resolving after discontinuation.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Liver failure is reported with **valproate**, **lamotrigine**, **topiramate** and **carbamazepine**; risk factors are young age and combination therapy. Two mechanisms: metabolic toxicity (e.g. 4-en **valproate** metabolite) and hypersensitivity (dose-independent, giving fulminant failure). Severe hepatic damage with **valproate** is seen especially in those with learning disability when undiagnosed urea cycle disorders are present (often under 2 years of age).

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Acute pancreatitis is a rare **valproate** effect; it is a hypersensitivity reaction, so dose reduction will not help.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Hyperammonaemia can be associated with coarse tremor and **carbamazepine** co-prescription and may respond to L-carnitine; **valproate** competes with carnitine transport and can cause carnitine depletion, especially in children and epileptics.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.title: Valproate - polycystic ovaries (PCOD)
rows: 25-==33%== of **UK** adult females have **PCO** morphology on ultrasound; 5-==26%== have **PCOD** (**PCO** plus hyperandrogenism or **LH** disturbance)
==10%== of women on **valproate** have new-onset **PCOD**; relative risk 7.5; most remit on stopping
Exact mechanism unknown; **valproate** increases ovarian androgen production, can cause weight gain and insulin resistance, and in the liver can increase unbound testosterone
Epilepsy itself is tipped to increase **PCOD**; such an association has not been established for bipolar disorder
Almost all patients who develop oligomenorrhoea do so in the first year of **valproate**

sources.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **Valproate** teratogenicity: neural tube defects in ==1%== to ==4%== of mothers; folate-vitamin B complex supplementation for all young women of childbearing potential may reduce risk, though it is best to avoid **valproate** totally. Learning disability and low **IQ** in children is the most common teratogenic effect of **valproate**.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **Valproate** can cause obesity, hyperandrogenism and **PCOD** associated with hirsutism.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.title: Anticonvulsant hypersensitivity, rash and Stevens-Johnson syndrome
rows: Seen in ==0.1%== of patients taking anticonvulsants; aromatic compounds (**lamotrigine**, **carbamazepine**, **phenytoin**, phenobarbitone) are especially risky
5 to ==20%== of those on aromatic anticonvulsants; **lamotrigine** rash in ==10%== of patients
Rapid initial dose escalation, concurrent **valproate**, age less than 16 years
Benign rashes cannot be distinguished from serious ones, so any rash requires discontinuation of the drug

**Lamotrigine** risk ==1 in 3000==, especially with **valproate** (enzyme inhibition raises **lamotrigine** levels); starts with rash, pharyngitis and fever; systemic involvement follows quickly if the drug is not stopped

sources.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.title: Weight-related effects
rows: Weight gain in ==70%== over 12 months; due to impaired beta-oxidation of fatty acids, independent of calorie intake
Weight neutral, can even cause weight loss; potentially used to counteract weight gain from many psychotropics

sources.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **Q25**: fatal skin problem with **lamotrigine** = Stevens-Johnson syndrome; bank says 10-==14%== develop rash (most benign), most likely in the first 2-8 weeks, more likely with **valproate**, exceeding the starting dose or rapid escalation (notes: ==10%==; risk factors as above).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Q27**: drug associated with nephrolithiasis = **topiramate** (low bicarbonate, renal calculi in about ==1.5%== of cases).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Q50**: **topiramate** can cause appetite suppression and weight loss (**valproate**, **lithium** and **lamotrigine** are not the answer).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Q71**: mood stabiliser that progressed from rash to Stevens-Johnson syndrome = **lamotrigine**.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

blocks.note: **Q9** keys diarrhoea (**GI** effects - nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, diarrhoea - most common in the first month, especially with rapid dose increase) as the most common **valproate** adverse effect. The notes do not state which effect is commonest.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

bullets.text: Carbamazepine dose-related: visual, GI, cognitive, vertigo; idiosyncratic: agranulocytosis/aplastic anaemia, SJS, hepatic failure, pancreatitis. Valproate dose-related: hyperammonaemia, teratogenicity, sedation, thrombocytopenia; idiosyncratic: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, rash.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Valproate liver: transaminitis in 5-40% (up to 3x ULN); fulminant failure by hypersensitivity (young age, combination, urea cycle disorders in learning disability); pancreatitis = hypersensitivity.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Valproate PCOD: 10% of women, relative risk 7.5, remits on stopping; oligomenorrhoea in the first year.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Valproate teratogenicity: neural tube defects in 1-4%; learning disability/low IQ commonest teratogenic effect.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Carbamazepine leucopenia in about 10% in first 3 months; thrombocytopenia with valproate and carbamazepine is dose-related.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Any rash: stop. Lamotrigine rash 10%, SJS 1 in 3000, worse with valproate, rapid escalation, age under 16.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Weight: valproate 70% and carbamazepine 40% over 12 months; lamotrigine often weight neutral; topiramate neutral or weight loss.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

bullets.text: Topiramate: word-finding difficulty and poor concentration; vigabatrin: visual field defects; lamotrigine: dizziness, ataxia, headache, sedation, tremor, nausea.

sections.title: 6. Other agents - cholinesterase inhibitors, ADHD drugs and hypnotics

blocks.text: Cholinesterase inhibitors: **donepezil** commonly causes nausea, diarrhoea, insomnia, vomiting and muscle cramps; **rivastigmine** causes similar symptoms, at a higher frequency for some; **galantamine** has a similar profile. Tacrine is no longer used in the **UK** because of reports of fatal hepatotoxicity.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.title: Further effects of cholinesterase inhibitors (increased central and peripheral cholinergic stimulation)
rows: Increase the risk of **GI** bleeding, especially in **NSAID** users or patients with peptic ulcer
Bradycardia, especially in those with supraventricular conduction delay
Prolong the effects of succinylcholine-type muscle relaxants

sources.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **Rivastigmine**'s metabolism does not depend on liver **P450** enzymes, so no **P450**-related interactions have been observed. **Memantine** does not inhibit or induce hepatic microsomal enzymes and is excreted in urine mostly unchanged, so it is unlikely to be affected by drugs altering hepatic enzyme function.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Stimulants and other **ADHD** drugs: commonest effects are anxiety, irritability, insomnia, tachycardia, cardiac arrhythmias and dysphoria with decreased appetite (tolerance usually develops for appetite loss). Less commonly, self-limited exacerbation of tics and dyskinesias.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Stimulants are linked to growth suppression; bruxism and restlessness also reported. Pemoline is associated with fulminant hepatic failure and is no longer widely used. Dependence can occur with **methylphenidate**, though rarely at **ADHD** doses.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: **Atomoxetine**: appetite loss, sexual dysfunction and dizziness; severe liver injury has also been reported. **Clonidine** is not popular for tics/**ADHD** because of high rates of hypotension.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Benzodiazepine overdose: slurred speech, incoordination, unsteady gait, nystagmus, impairment of attention or memory, stupor or coma, and behavioural changes (inappropriate sexual or aggressive behaviour, mood lability, impaired judgment).

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: High-potency benzodiazepines such as triazolam can cause anterograde amnesia. Paradoxical disinhibition is seen in a few patients, especially with pre-existing brain damage; triazolam has been banned in the **UK** since 1991 after reports of disinhibition and aggression.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Benzodiazepines can produce respiratory impairment, especially in **COPD** or sleep apnoea, and are better avoided in myasthenia gravis, head injury or porphyria. **Alprazolam** can cause weight gain via appetite stimulation.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Teratogenic/neonatal: cleft palate and lip are associated with benzodiazepines; a withdrawal syndrome is seen in neonates after third trimester use. Z-hypnotics cause more stomach upset and diarrhoea than benzodiazepines; eszopiclone's unique temporary side effect is an unpleasant taste, and it can cause dose-dependent dry mouth in the elderly.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Benzodiazepine withdrawal depends on duration of treatment, dosage, rate of tapering and half-life of the compound. It is characterised by anxiety, diaphoresis, kinaesthetic hallucinations, restlessness, irritability, light-headedness, tremor, insomnia, autonomic hyperactivity and weakness; in severe cases depression, paranoia, delirium and grand mal seizures. It can occur after 1 or 2 weeks with long-acting benzodiazepines; **alprazolam** and **lorazepam** give immediate and severe withdrawal and should be tapered gradually.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.title: Benzodiazepine withdrawal and dependence by duration of use (Law et al. 2004, as cited in the notes)

sources.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.text: Strategies for withdrawal: slow taper at ==25%== per week, longer-acting agents when tapering, avoiding long-term use of short-acting benzodiazepines, and **carbamazepine** to assist discontinuation.

source.file: paper-a/MRCPSYCH PAPER A SECTIONS/ADVERSE DRUG EFFECTS.pdf

blocks.title: Notes vs question bank - cholinesterase inhibitors

items.text: Notes list urinary retention among the effects of cholinesterase inhibitors. **Q58** is keyed with urinary retention as the option that is **NOT** a recognised side effect (explanation: they cause urinary incontinence, not retention; also nausea ==11%==-==47%==, vomiting ==10%==-==31%==, diarrhoea ==5%==-==19%==, anorexia ==4%==-==17%==, cramps, bradycardia with **donepezil**). Direct disagreement - flag to check.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

items.text: **Q21**: constipation is **NOT** a common **rivastigmine** side effect (very rare).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Q39**: commonest side effect of **methylphenidate** = insomnia (also appetite suppression, raised **BP** and pulse, growth deceleration).

source.file: paper-a/High yields/PHARMACOLOGY/Adverse effects Attempt review.pdf
